questions.problem: What is the length of the longer leg in a ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle if the hypotenuse has a length of $2?$
questions.worked_solution:

Since the hypotenuse has a length of $2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =2 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now calculate the length of the longer leg as follows:

$$
\sqrt{3}x=\sqrt{3}\cdot 1=\sqrt{3}
$$

Therefore, the longer leg has a length of $\sqrt{3}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14165760/assets/d162f5a85434a7798dd29a42bb45dd801d38560f6ad1aeea090c9d371a024dd2.png)

Given that the triangle $△ABC$ above is an equilateral triangle and $AH=40,$ what is the length of $\overset{―}{AC}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's draw triangle $△ABH,$ which is a ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14165760/assets/7cbfe29dd9087d07b6d2101e85b9154836704221320f4dd19346f49f3a858fa3.png)

 

Since the longer leg, $\overset{―}{AH},$ has a length of $40,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}x & =40 \\ x & =\frac{40}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{40}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{40\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We can now calculate the length of the hypotenuse, $\overset{―}{AB},$ as follows:

$$
AB=2x=2\cdot \frac{40\sqrt{3}}{3}=\frac{80\sqrt{3}}{3}.
$$

Finally, since $△ABC$ is an equilateral triangle, we get

$$
AC=AB=\frac{80\sqrt{3}}{3}.
$$

Example: 
                    Relating the Length of the Shorter Leg to the Length of the Longer Leg
canonical_examples.problem:
In the triangle below, what is the length of the shorter leg?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14165760/assets/aeb29243195210194a1f114fdf5146bcbd418180c957d5a1c88c3f1055a5c5c9.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's refer to our standard $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14165760/assets/58993cc083d8561501ea9db70c6d4d886fadc4d4ac3455a1a58de1fe5ceb6e77.png)

Since this is a $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle, the length of the longer leg is $\sqrt{3}$ times that of the shorter leg.

Here, the longer leg has length $2,$ and the shorter leg has length $x,$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\sqrt{3}x \\ x & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the radical from the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and denominator by the radical:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{2\cdot \sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{3}}=\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the length of the shorter leg is $\dfrac{2 \sqrt{3}}{3}.$

Since the hypotenuse has a length of $6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =6 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we know $x,$ we can calculate the length of the longer leg as follows:

$$
\sqrt{3}x = \sqrt{3} \cdot 3 = 3\sqrt{3}.
$$

Therefore, the longer leg has a length of $3 \sqrt{3}.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Let's consider an equilateral triangle with sides of length $2x$. Notice that any altitude will split it into two congruent triangles, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14165760/assets/301fe26a314d91d0d316758a5076cea2383f325991789addceaec71f0e7b16dd.png)

In the new smaller triangle the acute angles will be $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ.$ Such triangles are called **$\boldsymbol{30^\circ}$-$\boldsymbol{60^\circ}$-$\boldsymbol{90^\circ}$ triangles**.

Based on the picture above, we see a special property shared by all $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangles:

*In any ${30^\circ}$-${60^\circ}$-${90^\circ}$ triangle, the hypotenuse is twice as long as the shortest leg (which is opposite the $30^\circ$ angle).*

This also works in the other direction:

*If the hypotenuse is twice as long as the shortest leg, then the given right triangle is a ${30^\circ}$-${60^\circ}$-${90^\circ}$ triangle.*

tutorials.name: The Longer Leg
tutorials.problem:
Consider the same ${30^\circ}$-${60^\circ}$-${90^\circ}$ triangle from before. This time, however, we will focus on the height ($h$) instead of the hypotenuse.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14165760/assets/301fe26a314d91d0d316758a5076cea2383f325991789addceaec71f0e7b16dd.png)

Applying the Pythagorean Theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(2x)^{2} & ={x}^{2}+{h}^{2} \\ {h}^{2} & =4{x}^{2}-{x}^{2} \\ {h}^{2} & =3{x}^{2} \\ h & =\sqrt{3}x,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives us the second important property:

*In any ${30^\circ}$-${60^\circ}$-${90^\circ}$ triangle, the length of the longer leg (which is opposite the $60^\circ$ angle) is $\sqrt{3}$ times the length of the shorter leg (which is opposite the $30^\circ$ angle).*
